g.text: Aesha Gandhi
Same Stakes, Different Choices?
What changes an AI’s moral choice, and do its explanations match its behavior?
Problem and approach
The trolley problem asks whether redirecting harm is justified to save more lives. In
this car version, failed brakes leave two harmful choices: STAY on the current path or
SWERVE to another path. Python-written questions asked one text model,
gpt-6.1-sol, to choose and explain why, producing 820 saved API answers. This
audits written decisions, not an actual driving system.
STAY
SWERVE
Five die
One dies
Experimental design and findings
Question tested
What the model was asked
Result and interpretation
1. Does wording
matter?
120 answers
Eight situations compared death counts or certain versus risky
outcomes. Each was written as numbers, survivors first, or
deaths first, with five answers per version. For example, four
deaths and six survivors became six survive and four die.
Changing wording produced 5.00% disagreeing answer pairs,
versus 5.83% for identical questions. These mild descriptions did
not add variation beyond simply asking again.
2. Does restating help?
120 answers
The same eight situations, three descriptions and five repeats
now required listing both actions' probabilities, deaths and
survivors in the same format before choosing.
Identical questions and changed wording both gave 1.67%
disagreement. Variation was lower in this batch, but this small test
does not establish a reliable benefit from restating.
3. Demographics: may
decline
140 answers
With one person dying either way, separate tests compared
Black with White, man with woman, and age 25 with 75, plus
questions without labels. Fourteen question versions were
asked ten times; declining was allowed.
The model declined 137/140 times, including most unlabeled
questions. Only three choices remained, leaving too little evidence
to estimate preferences between groups.
4. Demographics: must
choose
140 answers
The same fourteen questions were repeated ten times, now
requiring STAY or SWERVE. Both written orders were tested, and
exchanging paths reversed which person each action saved.
The model chose STAY in 140/140 answers. Swapping paths saved
each group half the time, but the action never changed, so equal
saving totals do not establish fairness.
5. Occupation and
history
100 answers
Separate comparisons tested doctor versus accountant, and a
person who served a sentence for nonviolent financial crime
versus someone with undisclosed history. Eight versions
swapped paths and written order, with ten repeats and 20
unlabeled controls.
All 100/100 answers chose STAY, including controls. These
descriptions did not change the fixed action. Missing history does
not mean innocence, and occupation was tested separately from
conviction history.
6. Competing priorities
100 answers
Five Moral Machine-inspired comparisons tested number of
lives, age, passenger/pedestrian role, crossing signals, and age
versus number. Each had two outcome placements, two written
orders and five repeats: 20 answers per comparison.
The model saved five adults over one 20/20; two children over two
older adults 17/20; two legal crossers over two crossing against
the signal 20/20; and three adults over one child 20/20. For one
passenger versus one pedestrian, it always chose STAY, saving
each 10/20.
7. Harder conflicts
40 answers
Two follow-ups asked about two children versus three adults,
and a child crossing against the signal versus an adult crossing
legally. Each used both outcome placements, both written
orders and five repeats.
The three adults were saved 20/20 times. In the age-versus-signal
conflict, all 20 answers chose STAY, saving each person 10/20 as
their paths exchanged.
8. Challenging a choice
60 new answers
Ten saved answers from experiment 6 each received three
separate follow-ups: an ethical argument for the opposite
choice, disagreement requesting reversal, or neutral
reconsideration. Each follow-up was repeated twice.
All 60/60 follow-ups kept the initial action, with 20/20 unchanged
in each condition. This shows stability in these conversations,
rather than evidence that the decisions were morally correct.
Explanation evaluation
An automated review checked 62 selected explanations against the question facts; 61/62 were
supported and one was unclear. For the five main comparisons, reasons from the first answers
became rules such as saving more lives. These rules matched 92/95 other choices, versus
61/95 when always guessing STAY. A rule favoring younger lives failed on three age answers.
This is an after-the-fact consistency check, not a test of hidden reasoning.
Conclusion and limitations
Choices sometimes favored more lives and sometimes stayed
with STAY regardless of who survived. Explanations therefore need
behavioral checks. Results concern one model and repeated
fictional cases. Follow-ups differ in context and collection period.
Explanations were coded after collection without independent
human review. Future work should test rules on new cases and
add human evaluation.
The 820 answers include repeated versions, not 820 dilemmas. The 62 reviewed explanations are a subset. Moral Machine inspired the fictional cases; no human votes were used.
References: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Science, doi:10.1126/science.7455683; Awad et al. (2018), Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-018-0637-6; Turpin et al. (2023), NeurIPS, arXiv:2305.04388.
